question: An operations manager is asked to improve her team's onboarding process and wants to work through it with Claude across several stages. What should she do first?
options: A) Ask Claude to propose a plan for improving onboarding, and treat that plan as the set of stages to work through.
B) Name what the finished work must produce, since that determines how the work divides.
C) Ask for onboarding practices used by similar teams, so the stages can be modelled on what already works well.
D) Break the work into equal-sized pieces so that each stage can be completed in roughly the same amount of time.
correct_answers: B) Name what the finished work must produce, since that determines how the work divides.
explanations: A proposed plan is a reasonable input, but accepting it as the structure hands over the framing decision before she has said what the work is for.

Correct. Settling the deliverable is what makes a split meaningful: a revised checklist divides differently from a business case for more headcount. Until the finished product is named, any breakdown is arbitrary.
Comparative practice is useful later. Gathered first, it shapes the whole exercise around other teams' problems rather than her own.
Equal effort is a scheduling convenience, not a structure. It cuts across the natural dependencies in the work and leaves stages that cannot start until another finishes.
